strengths: The paper addresses a relevant speech-processing problem and proposes an interesting direction for bandwidth extension: using nonlinear-dynamics signals such as Lyapunov exponents and detrended fluctuation analysis to guide adversarial discriminators.

The dual-stream magnitude/phase generator combines cross-stream information exchange, local convolutional modeling, and global self-attention, with an explicit residual mechanism for high-frequency recovery.
The empirical study includes several complementary objective metrics, discriminator and generator ablations, multiple input-frequency ranges, and computational-complexity measurements.
The model appears parameter-efficient relative to large recent baselines, and depthwise-separable convolutions are used to reduce discriminator cost.
Pseudocode for MRLD and MSDFA, use of the public VCTK corpus, and some training/environment details provide a partial basis for reproduction.
weaknesses: The central state-of-the-art claim is not supported by the reported results. For example, lower LSD is better, yet NDSI-BWE reports 0.98/0.79/0.79 while several baseline rows report lower values such as 0.96/0.74/0.75 and 0.72/0.72/0.73. STOI is also tied rather than improved on several ranges. The textual interpretation therefore contradicts Table 3.

The abstract claims a subjective evaluation with five human judges, but the paper provides no listening-test protocol, listener information, stimuli, ratings, statistical analysis, or subjective results. The only MOS-like reported measure is NISQA-MOS, an automatic reference-free predictor.

The claimed discriminator contributions are inconsistent and incompletely described. The abstract says there are four new discriminators but lists seven named components; MS-RD and MR-PPD are introduced by name but never defined in the method section, while MPD, MRAD, and MRPD appear to be prior components.

Key reproducibility details are missing, including the full training objective, adversarial and reconstruction loss formulations, loss weights, data splits, differentiability of nearest-neighbor Lyapunov and DFA computations, and several architecture details. No code or model release is provided.

The empirical evidence is narrow: all experiments use only the English, read-speech, noise-free VCTK corpus. Generalization to noisy speech, other datasets, cross-lingual speakers, low-resource conditions, or real telephone channels is not established.

The conceptual claim that the proposed measures explicitly capture deterministic chaos in speech is not directly validated. Better downstream metrics do not by themselves show that the discriminators measure chaotic dynamics rather than other statistical regularities.
No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported, so it is unclear whether the small differences among the best models are reliable.

Presentation quality needs substantial improvement. Figures 2 and 3 are labeled 'Dummy' and appear duplicated, citations are left as '(?)', and there are numerous grammar and spelling errors such as 'genetor,' 'benchmakr,' 'supression,' and 'paramterter.' The term 'complex-valued' is also used loosely because the main streams appear to process real-valued magnitude and phase representations separately.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practical speech-processing problem: bandwidth extension with explicit magnitude and phase reconstruction.
The dual-stream generator combining Lattice-Net cross-stream interaction, Conformer-style global modeling, and ConvNeXt-style local processing is a plausible and coherent architectural direction.
Introducing Lyapunov-exponent and detrended-fluctuation analyses into adversarial discriminators is an interesting attempt to provide nonlinear dynamical inductive biases for audio generation.
The evaluation includes several complementary objective metrics, discriminator and generator ablations, multiple frequency ranges, and computational-cost measurements.
The reported use of depthwise-separable convolutions and a relatively compact 33.5M-parameter generator suggests a potentially useful efficiency contribution, subject to verification.
weaknesses: The central claims are not adequately supported. The abstract mentions a subjective evaluation by five human judges, but no listening-test protocol, participant details, questionnaire, or subjective results are presented. NISQA is an objective/no-reference predictor, not a human MOS score.

The empirical case for state-of-the-art performance is narrow and fragile. All experiments appear to use only the noise-free English VCTK corpus, with unclear train/validation/test splits, no statistical significance testing, no multiple-seed analysis, and no external or noisy/multilingual evaluation.

There are major inconsistencies in the claimed contributions. The abstract alternates between four new discriminators and seven discriminators and names MS-RD and MR-PPD, which are never formally defined or used in the described experiments. The body and tables appear to involve only five discriminators.

The proposed MRLD is not reproducible from Algorithm 1: the nearest neighbor y'_j, embedding dimension d, delay tau, divergence horizon Delta, neighbor-exclusion rule, and boundary handling are undefined. Lyapunov estimation also raises stationarity and trajectory-length concerns that are not addressed.

The MSDFA description is similarly incomplete. DFA normally produces a fluctuation statistic F(n) for each scale, but the algorithm says to tile this scalar into an S x S map without defining S, local segmentation, detrending, or the tiling operation.

The paper does not demonstrate that either discriminator actually measures deterministic chaos or fractal dynamics. There are no controlled synthetic tests, surrogate-data analyses, feature visualizations, or ablations separating the proposed nonlinear interpretation from ordinary CNN feature extraction.

Essential training details are missing, including the complete adversarial loss, reconstruction loss, feature-matching loss, loss weights, discriminator balancing, optimizer settings for all components, STFT parameters, channel dimensions, and several generator/discriminator implementation details. MRAD and MRPD are largely delegated to an external paper.

Reported numerical results are internally inconsistent. For example, the 2-16 kHz PESQ score appears as 1.66 in Table 1 but 1.166 in Table 4. As printed, Table 3 also contradicts the prose: NDSI-BWE appears worse than a baseline in LSD for several ranges and lower in STOI for the 4-16 kHz setting, despite the claim of superiority on all those metrics.

Parameter-reduction claims are confusing and inconsistent across the paper. The abstract claims an eight-times reduction, Table 3 indicates roughly 2.18x and 1.28x reductions relative to AP-BWE and MS-BWE, while other passages claim 40x, 20x, and approximately 0.05x reductions for different components without clear framing.

The baseline study is not transparent: several entries appear missing, and it is unclear whether published numbers or retrained models were used, whether preprocessing was matched, or whether model capacities and training budgets were controlled.

The presentation is below publication quality. The introduction begins abruptly with 'However'; the related-work section promises a nonlinear-dynamical-systems review that is absent; citations appear as '(?)'; Figure 1 does not clearly match the textual architecture; and Figures 2 and 3 are duplicated and captioned 'Dummy'. There are also numerous notation errors and typos.

Because of the unsupported subjective claims, incomplete mathematical definitions, contradictory tables, and limited generalization evidence, the current submission does not meet the soundness and reproducibility threshold for Findings. Substantial new experimentation, clarification, and manuscript reconstruction are required.

strengths: Addresses a relevant speech-processing problem, bandwidth extension, with clear relevance to TTS, ASR, and natural-sounding speech generation.

Combines magnitude and phase modeling through a dual-stream ConformerNeXt/Lattice generator; the architecture is detailed and the ablations support the value of cross-stream interaction and the ConformerNeXt block.

Introduces two unconventional discriminator inputs based on Lyapunov-exponent and detrended-fluctuation features. Although the chaos interpretation is not fully established, the discriminator ablations indicate that these features provide useful additional supervision.

Evaluation is comparatively broad: three bandwidth regimes, six objective metrics, human MOS and preference tests, discriminator and generator ablations, parameter counts, MACs/FLOPs, and RTF are reported.
The proposed system achieves better perceptual-quality metrics than AP-BWE—particularly NISQA-MOS, LSD, PESQ, and STOI—while using roughly half the total model parameters.
The appendix supplies useful reproducibility material, including preprocessing, pseudocode, training hyperparameters, inference steps, and layer-wise parameter tables.
The authors explicitly acknowledge important limitations concerning the single dataset, English-only data, and noise-free evaluation.
weaknesses: The central claim that MRLD and MSDFA specifically model deterministic chaos is not directly validated. Lyapunov estimates and DFA can also respond to nonstationarity, turbulence, or long-range correlation; synthetic chaotic-system sanity checks, feature analyses, or interpretability experiments are needed to substantiate the chaos interpretation.

Evaluation is limited to VCTK under clean, English-only conditions. There is no cross-dataset, cross-language, noisy, reverberant, telephone-channel, or downstream ASR evaluation, despite ASR being emphasized in the motivation.

Statistical evidence is weak. No standard deviations, confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-seed results are provided. Several gains over AP-BWE are small, and AP-BWE is actually slightly better on SI-SDR and SI-SNR for all three reported ranges.

The subjective study uses only ten demographically homogeneous, non-native-English listeners. The preference result is also reported inconsistently: Section 3.11 says an 11% margin over AP-BWE, while Appendix A.9 says 2%. The appendix additionally claims noisy and reverberant conditions that are not part of the experimental design.

Reproducibility is only partially adequate. No code, checkpoint, or sample-release link is provided, and important MRLD details are missing, including embedding dimension, delay, divergence horizon, and nearest-neighbor exclusion criteria. Some loss weights, exact speaker splits, and model-selection procedures are also unclear.

The 40x discriminator-reduction claim is potentially misleading. It compares only MRLD+MSDFA (483.2k) with MPD (22M), whereas the full discriminator also contains MRAD and MRPD and totals about 1.68M parameters, roughly a 14x reduction from the complete MPD-based suite. The abstract should state precisely what is being compared.

There are architecture-description inconsistencies. MRLD is described in the text as using 2D convolutions, but Table 7 reports Conv1d layers. The sense in which the system is genuinely complex-valued, as opposed to processing real magnitude and phase streams, also needs clarification.

Baseline comparison could be stronger. Only three baselines are included, and the very large capacity mismatch between MPD and the chaos discriminators raises fairness questions unless matched-capacity controls or reimplementation details are provided. Diffusion-based and other recent generative BWE systems are not compared.

Some related-work statements are overbroad, such as claiming that traditional methods cannot model chaotic dynamics and that neural methods generally neglect phase, despite citing phase-aware approaches.

The phrase in the abstract implying better performance across all eight metrics should be qualified: the model improves perceptual and several reconstruction metrics but does not improve SI-SDR or SI-SNR relative to the strongest baseline.
